clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive, usually complicated (occasionally pure) hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic variants in CYP2U1, a cytochrome P450 fatty-acid hydroxylase acting on arachidonic acid and other long-chain fatty acids.
Early onset in infancy or early childhood, frequently with cognitive impairment and dystonia in addition to lower-limb spasticity.
Characteristic imaging clues include bilateral basal-ganglia (particularly pallidal) calcification, a thin corpus callosum and white-matter hyperintensities.
A subclinical sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and pes cavus are commonly found on detailed assessment.
SPG56 is one of the fatty-acid-metabolism complicated spastic paraplegias, sharing biochemical themes with FA2H (SPG35) and the DDHD phospholipase subtypes.
Impaired hydroxylation of arachidonic acid and related fatty acids links CYP2U1 to eicosanoid and fatty-acid signalling in the nervous system.
Beyond fatty-acid hydroxylation, secondary mitochondrial dysfunction with altered coenzyme Q metabolism has been implicated in CYP2U1 disease.
reference.pathophysiology: CYP2U1 encodes a highly conserved cytochrome P450 enzyme (family 2, subfamily U) that functions as a fatty-acid hydroxylase, metabolising arachidonic acid, docosahexaenoic acid and other long-chain fatty acids into hydroxylated signalling molecules. Biallelic loss-of-function variants impair this hydroxylation and perturb lipid and eicosanoid signalling, and available evidence indicates a secondary disturbance of mitochondrial function and coenzyme Q homeostasis. The resulting length-dependent corticospinal degeneration is accompanied in many individuals by basal-ganglia calcification, white-matter change and a thin corpus callosum, giving the disorder its complicated phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Primary familial brain calcification (e.g. SLC20A2, PDGFB, PDGFRB), given the basal-ganglia calcification
SPG35 (FA2H) — a fatty-acid hydroxylase complicated form and the closest biochemical sibling
SPG54 (DDHD2), SPG28 (DDHD1) and SPG46 (GBA2) — other lipid-metabolism complicated spastic paraplegias
SPG11 (spatacsin) and SPG15 (spastizin) — early-onset complicated forms with thin corpus callosum
Mitochondrial leukoencephalopathies and coenzyme Q deficiency states
additionalInvestigations: Gene panel or exome sequencing to confirm biallelic CYP2U1 variants with segregation studies
Brain CT, which is sensitive for basal-ganglia calcification, alongside MRI for white-matter and corpus callosum assessment
Nerve conduction studies to detect subclinical axonal neuropathy
Metabolic work-up for mitochondrial and coenzyme Q markers where available
Calcium, phosphate and parathyroid screen interpreted qualitatively to exclude other causes of intracranial calcification
redFlags: Progressive dystonia or other movement disorder
Extensive intracranial calcification prompting exclusion of metabolic or endocrine causes
Loss of independent walking during childhood
reference.prognosis: The disorder is early in onset and slowly progressive; walking is often affected in childhood and many individuals need aids, with cognitive and extrapyramidal involvement adding disability, though the overall course is chronic.
pitfalls: Attributing basal-ganglia calcification to primary familial brain calcification or to a calcium or parathyroid disorder and thereby missing CYP2U1 disease
Relying on MRI alone, which is insensitive to calcification, when CT is needed
Misdiagnosis as cerebral palsy given the early onset
Missing a subclinical neuropathy in the absence of nerve conduction studies
references: Hereditary spastic paraplegia clinical and genetic reviews
